a little in front of the sea. But then Lynceus alone
thought he saw Heracles far off over the boundless land,
seeing him as one on the first day of the month sees the moon,
or thinks he sees it through cloud.
And going back to his comrades he told them that no other
searcher going forth would overtake him; and they too
came back, both swift-footed Euphemus and the two sons
of Thracian Boreas, having toiled in vain.

But you, Canthus, the deadly Fates took in Libya.
You met flocks at pasture; and there followed a man,
their shepherd, who, while you would bring them to your comrades
in their need, defending his own sheep, slew you,
striking you with a stone; for he was no weakling,
the grandson of Phoebus Lycoreius, Caphaurus,
and of modest Acacallis, whom once Minos
sent away to Libya, bearing the heavy seed of the god,
his own daughter; and she bore a splendid son to Phoebus,
whom they call Amphithemis and Garamas.
And Amphithemis then lay with a Tritonian nymph;
and she bore him Nasamon and strong Caphaurus,
who then slew Canthus over his sheep.
Nor did he escape the harsh hands of the chieftains,
when they learned what he had done. And the corpse afterward they took up,
the Minyae, when they had learned, and buried it in the earth,
mourning; and the flocks they brought back with them.

There too on the same day a pitiless doom seized
the son of Ampycus, Mopsus; nor did he escape his bitter fate
by his prophecies; for there is no turning aside of death.
There lay upon the sands, shunning the midday heat,
a dread serpent, sluggish indeed to harm one who is unwilling,
nor would it dart at one who shrank back in fear.
But into whomever, of all the living things that the life-giving
earth nourishes with breath, it first should send its black venom,
the road to Hades was not so much as a cubit;
no, not if Paean—if it is right for me to say it openly—
should heal him, if only it had grazed him with its teeth.
For when godlike Perseus flew over Libya,
Eurymedon—for by that name too his mother called him—
bearing to the king the freshly severed head of the Gorgon,
all the drops of dark blood that fell to the ground
sprang up into a brood of those serpents.
On the tip of its spine Mopsus set
his left foot, putting it forward; and it, twisting
in agony, bit and tore the muscle and the flesh
of the middle of his shin. And Medea and the other
handmaids fled in terror; but he stroked the bloody wound
boldly, for no overwhelming pain yet tormented him.
Wretched one! Already beneath his skin there crept a deadly
limb-loosening torpor, and a great mist poured over his eyes.
And straightway sinking down on the ground, his limbs grown heavy,
he grew cold in helplessness; and his comrades gathered round him,
and the hero Aeson's son, amazed at the bitter calamity.
Nor even for a little while, though dead, was he
to lie beneath the sun. For the venom at once made his flesh
rot within, and the hair, dissolving, fell from his skin.
And quickly with bronze mattocks they dug a deep grave
in haste; and they tore their hair,
themselves and the maidens, mourning piteously
for the dead man who had suffered so; and three times marching round him with their arms,
having duly given him funeral rites, they laid him beneath a heaped mound of earth.

But when they had embarked upon the ship, as the south wind blew
over the sea, and they sought out the passages
to come out of the Tritonian lake, having no plan
for a long while, but heedlessly all the day they were borne about.
And as a serpent goes its winding way,
when the keenest blaze of the sun warms it,
and with a hiss it turns its head this way and that, and its eyes
flash like sparks of fire as it rages,
until it slips into its hole through a cleft;
so Argo, seeking the navigable mouth of the lake,
wandered about for a long time. And at once Orpheus
bade them set Apollo's great tripod outside the ship
to the native gods, as an offering for their homecoming.
And they set down the treasure of Phoebus, stepping onto the land;
and to them, in the likeness of a youth, there appeared
broad-mighty Triton, and lifting up a clod of earth
he held it out as a guest-gift to the chieftains, and spoke:
"Take it, friends; since I have here no surpassing
guest-gift to give you now as you meet me.
But if you seek the passages of this sea, such things as men
often need when they journey in a foreign land,
I will tell you. For my father Poseidon has made me
to be knowing of this sea. And I rule
the coast, if you have heard, dwelling far off,
of Eurypylus, born in Libya, the nurse of wild beasts."

So he spoke; and Euphemus readily held out his hands for the clod,
and spoke thus in answer:
"If you know aught, hero, of Apis and the Minoan
sea, tell us truly as we ask.
For not willingly do we come hither, but driven by heavy
storms onto the bounds of this land,
we carried our ship aloft into this stream of the lake
across the mainland, weighed down; nor do we at all know
where the voyage leads out to reach the land of Pelops."

So he spoke; and Triton stretched out his hand, and pointed afar,
speaking, to the sea and the deep mouth of the lake:
"That is the outlet of the sea, where most
the unmoving deep grows dark; on either side white
breakers bristle, gleaming; and between
the breakers a narrow path lies to drive out.
And that sea, stretching up misty, into the sacred land of Pelops
extends, beyond Crete; but, keeping to your right
hand, when from the lake you cast into the swell of the sea,
hold your course close along the shore,
as long as it stretches upward; but where the land,
sloping round, bends to the other side, then your voyage is safe
as you go straight from the jutting headland.
But go gladly, and let no weariness be your grief,
that your limbs, in the flower of youth, must toil."

He spoke kindly; and they at once went aboard the ship,
eager to come out of the lake by rowing.
And they sped on eagerly; but meanwhile Triton,
taking up the great tripod, was seen to go down
into the lake; and afterward no one saw him, so suddenly
he vanished, with the tripod, close at hand. And their hearts
were warmed, that one of the blessed gods had met them auspiciously.
And they bade Aeson's son slay the best of the sheep
of all the others and pray, when he had taken it.
And quickly he chose one in haste, and lifting it up
he slew it over the stern, and spoke with prayers:
"Divinity, whoever you are who appeared on the bounds
of this lake, whether men call you Triton, the sea-marvel,
or Phorcys, or the daughters of Nereus, the brides of the sea,
be gracious, and grant a sweet end to our homecoming."

He spoke, and with his prayers, cutting its throat, into the water
he cast it from the stern; and the god rose up from the deep,
such as in truth he was to behold.
And as when a man sends a swift horse into the broad ring
of the contest, grasping its shaggy and obedient mane,
and runs along beside it, while it, lifting its neck proudly,
follows, and the bright bits in its mouth
clatter, champed on either side as it bites them;
so he, grasping the keel of the hollow Argo,
led it on to the sea. And his body, from the topmost
head, about his back and his loins down to the belly,
was utterly like the blessed gods in its wondrous form;
but below his flanks the forked tail of a sea-monster
stretched out on this side and that; and he beat
the surface of the water with its spines, which below
divided into curving forks like the horns of the moon.
And he led her on, until he sent her on her way into the sea;
and quickly he sank into the great depth; and the heroes shouted,
beholding the dread marvel with their eyes.

There is the Argoan harbour, and the tokens of the ship,
and the altars of Poseidon and of Triton;
for that day they tarried. But at dawn,
with sails spread, keeping the desolate land
on their right, they sped on with the blast of the west wind.
And next at dawn they saw both the headland and the inmost sea
lying beyond the jutting cape.
And at once the west wind ceased, and there came the breeze
of the clear south wind; and they rejoiced in their hearts at its voice.
And when the sun set, and there rose the star
of the fold, which gives rest to the wretched ploughmen,
then, as the wind dropped in the dark night,
they loosed the sails and lowered the tall mast,
and laboured at the well-polished oars
all night long and through the day, and on the next day again
through another oncoming night. And far off rugged
Carpathos received them; and from there they were to cross over
to Crete, which rose above the other islands in the sea.
But Talos of bronze, breaking off rocks
from the stout crag, kept them from making fast their cables to the land,
as they came down to the Dictaean roadstead of the harbour.
He was of the bronze race of the men sprung from ash-trees,
the last left among the demigod men,
whom the son of Cronos gave to Europa to be the guardian of the island,
to circle Crete three times a day on his bronze feet.
Now all the rest of his body and his limbs were wrought
of bronze and unbreakable; but beneath the tendon at his ankle
was a blood-red duct; and this, with its thin membrane,
held the bounds of life and death.
And they, though sorely wearied with toil, at once from the land
drew back the ship in fear, backing water with their oars.
And miserably would they have been carried far from Crete,
toiling both with thirst and with their pains,
had not Medea spoken to them as they drew away:
"Hear me. For I alone, I think, can subdue for you
that man, whoever he is, even though he holds
a body all of bronze, unless his life be unwearied.
But keep the ship here, willingly, out of range
of the rocks, until he yields to be subdued by me."

So she spoke; and they drew the ship back out of range
of his missiles on their oars, awaiting what
plan she would work unlooked-for; and she, holding a fold of her purple
robe before her cheeks on either side,
stepped onto the deck; and clasping her hand with his,
Aeson's son led her as she went along the benches.
There with songs she sought to please, and chanted to the Fates,
the devourers of the soul, the swift hounds of Hades, who through all
the air, wheeling about, fall upon the living.
Kneeling, three times she called on them in songs,
three times in prayers; and setting an evil purpose, with hostile
eyes she bewitched the eyes of Talos of bronze;
and against him she gnashed her baleful wrath, and sent forth
destroying phantoms, raging with fury.

Father Zeus, truly great wonder rises in my mind,
if indeed not only by diseases and wounds does ruin
come upon us, but someone even from afar can do us harm.
So he, though of bronze, yielded to be subdued
by the might of much-drugged Medea. And as he lifted
heavy stones to keep them from reaching the harbour,
he grazed his ankle on a pointed rock; and the ichor
flowed from him like molten lead; nor long
did he stand, leaning upon the jutting crag.
But as some huge pine high in the mountains,
which woodmen, leaving it half-cut by their sharp axes,
have come down from the forest; and it in the night
first is shaken by gusts, and afterward
breaks off at the base and falls; so he upon his tireless
feet for a while stood swaying upright,
and then again, strengthless, fell with an immense crash.

So that night the heroes lodged there in Crete;
and after, as the dawn was newly shining,
they set up a shrine to Minoan Athena,
and drew water and went aboard, that they might
first of all ply their oars beyond the headland of Salmone.
But at once, as they sped over the great Cretan gulf,
night frightened them, that which they call the shroud of darkness;
no stars pierced that deadly night, nor the gleams
of the moon; but from heaven was black chaos, or some other
darkness rose up out of the innermost abysses.
And they themselves knew not at all whether they were borne
in Hades or on the waters; and they entrusted to the sea
their homecoming in helplessness, not knowing where it would carry them. But Jason,
lifting up his hands, with a great voice cried to Phoebus,
calling on him to save them; and tears streamed down
in his distress; and he promised many gifts to Pytho, many to Amyclae,
many beyond measure to bring to Ortygia.
Son of Leto, swiftly you came down from heaven to the Melantian
rocks, which lie in the sea,
keen to hear; and leaping upon one of the two,
you held aloft in your right hand your golden bow;
and the bow flashed a gleaming radiance all about.
And to them then a small island of the Sporades appeared
to see, opposite the little isle of Hippuris,
where they cast anchor and stayed; and at once Dawn
shone, rising; and they made for Apollo a splendid
precinct in a shady grove, and a shadowy altar,
calling on Phoebus the Gleamer for the sake of the watchful gleam;
and they named the smooth island Anaphe,
since Phoebus had revealed it to them in their dismay.
And they offered all that men can make ready to offer
on a desolate shore; and so, when with brands
they saw them pouring water as libations on the blazing offerings,
the Phaeacian handmaids of Medea could no longer
hold back the laughter in their breasts, since they had often
seen the slaughter of oxen in the house of Alcinous.
And the heroes pelted them with shameful words
in mockery, glad; and a sweet wrangling kindled among them,
and gibing strife. And from that
song of the heroes on the island even now in like manner the women
contend with the men, whenever with sacrifices they propitiate
Apollo the Gleamer, the guardian of Anaphe.

But when from there too they loosed the cables in fair weather,
then Euphemus remembered a dream of the night,
in reverence for the glorious son of Maia. For it seemed to him
that the divine clod, held at his breast in the crook of his arm,
was being watered with white drops of milk,
and that from the clod, small though it was,
there came a woman like a maiden; and joined with her in love
he was, in unbearable desire; and he lamented as though
he had wedded a girl whom he himself had reared on his own milk;
but she comforted him with gentle words:
"I am of the race of Triton, the nurse, dear friend, of your children,
not a girl; for Triton and Libya are my parents.
But set me with the daughters of Nereus,
to dwell in the sea near Anaphe; and I will come back to the rays
of the sun hereafter, ready for your descendants."

This his heart laid up in memory, and he told it
to Aeson's son; and he then, pondering in his mind the prophecies
of the Far-darter, lifted up his voice and spoke:
"Good friend, truly a great and splendid glory has fallen to you.
For the gods will make of this clod, when you cast it into the sea,
an island, where the children of your children
shall dwell; for Triton gave it you as a guest-gift,
this portion of the Libyan mainland. No other
of the immortals than he, who met you, gave it."

So he spoke; nor did Euphemus make void the answer
of Aeson's son; but, gladdened by the prophecies,
he cast the clod into the deep. And from it rose an island,
Calliste, the sacred nurse of the children of Euphemus,
who before once dwelt in Sintian Lemnos,
and being driven out of Lemnos by Tyrrhenian men
came to Sparta as guests; and from Sparta, when they left it,
the goodly son of Autesion, Theras, led them
to the fair island, and it changed its name to Thera
from him. But these things happened after the time of Euphemus.

From there, leaving behind countless swell of the sea,
they stayed upon the shores of Aegina; and at once
they contended in a blameless strife for the drawing of water,
who, having filled, should first reach the ship.
For both need and the boundless breeze urged them on.
There even now the youths of the Myrmidons, lifting
brimming jars upon their shoulders, with light
feet contend in a contest for victory.

Be gracious, race of the chieftains, the blessed; and may these songs
from year to year be sweeter to sing
to men. For now I come to the glorious end
of your toils; since no contest befell you any longer
as you returned again from Aegina,
nor did blasts of winds withstand you; but at your ease,
having measured the Cecropian land and Aulis
within Euboea, and the Opuntian cities of the Locrians,
gladly you stepped upon the Pagasaean shores.
